cards.text: Last time, she told the daughters of Jerusalem that her beloved had gone down to his garden, and she said, "I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me" (Song 6:3). Now he's the one talking, and he calls her "my darling." Friend, this man showed up with a LIST, and he is not reading it quietly.

cards.question: He tells his darling she's as beautiful as Tirzah, a city in Israel (1 Kings 15:33). Which other city does he say she's as lovely as?

cards.text: Then he says she's as majestic as troops with banners. Not a flower, friend. An ARMY with its flags flying.

cards.question: Next he asks his darling to turn her eyes away from him, because they have ___ him.
Then he says her hair is like a flock of animals streaming down from Gilead. Which animals?

cards.text: Now her teeth, like a flock of sheep coming up from the washing. Nobody's ever praised MY teeth, friend, because all I've got is a mustache and a dream.

cards.question: In his picture of her teeth, each sheep has its twin, and not one of them is lost.

cards.text: Then her brow behind her veil is like a slice of pomegranate. Goats, sheep, and now a fruit. This man is painting her a whole countryside, and he is NOT slowing down.
Now he brings up a crowd: sixty queens, eighty concubines and maidens without number.

cards.question: But next to all those queens, concubines and maidens, his dove, his perfect one, is ___.
His dove is the favorite of the mother who bore her.

cards.text: Now all those women get a look at his dove. My Minty's a dove, friend, so I already know how this goes.

cards.question: When the maidens see his dove, what do they do?

answers.text: They ask where she came from

cards.question: The queens and concubines are jealous of his dove.

cards.text: Then a question rings out about her, and the text leaves open who's asking. I bet they're as wide-eyed as I was the first night I saw the sky over my bakery.

cards.question: The question pictures her shining like what?

cards.text: The dawn, the moon, the sun and the stars in procession. My Berry would've had his face pressed to the kitchen window ALL night for this one.
Then a voice speaks, and the text doesn't say whose. It says, "I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley".

cards.question: At the walnut grove, the speaker went to see if the vines were ___ or the pomegranates were in bloom.

cards.text: Then the speaker says desire set them among the royal chariots of their people. One minute it's blossoms, the next minute it's CHARIOTS.

cards.question: The speaker knew exactly where that desire was leading the whole time.

cards.text: The speaker says it happened before they realized it. That's me with the oven timer, friend: I check ONE batch, and next thing I know I've boxed three hundred cookies.

findings.problem: The card opens with "Last time," which assumes this baker did the previous lesson. Papa Dorin isn't told how a baker has done before, and the previous passage is context only.

rule.text: What he doesn't know: anything about the individual baker that he hasn't been told, such as their streak, their mood, the time of day or how they've done before. In lessons, he's never told, because every baker gets the same lesson.

findings.problem: The card says her beloved had gone down to his garden. That fact is from Song of Solomon 6:2 and has no reference. The only inline reference is (Song 6:3), for the quote.

rule.text: References. Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The quote "I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me" doesn't appear to match the BSB, which reads "I belong to my beloved and my beloved belongs to me" (Song of Solomon 6:3). Verse 6:3 is outside the provided passage text, so the script may not have checked it. Check it against the BSB data. Use the exact wording or drop the quotation marks.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included. A paraphrase uses no quotation marks.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: "Then he says she's as majestic as troops with banners." "Not a flower, friend." "An ARMY with its flags flying."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess which animal is in the hair image (goats, quail or camels). Nothing earlier lets the baker reason it out. This is the same kind of detail-guessing as the Psalm 23 oil example the docs mark as bad. Ask about what the picture means or does instead.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says. Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The true or false card restates the exact next words of the line ("each has its twin, and not one of them is lost"). The baker can only guess whether the wording is right. It doesn't test the meaning of the image, such as a full, matched set with nothing missing.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: the brow line, "Goats, sheep, and now a fruit." and "This man is painting her a whole countryside, and he is NOT slowing down."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card cites Song of Solomon 6:5-7, but the only new moment it tells is 6:7 (the brow behind the veil). The goats (6:5) and sheep (6:6) only come up again as a recap. The citation should be Song of Solomon 6:7.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The question "His dove is the favorite of the mother who bore her" uses "His" to point back to a speaker set up on earlier cards. The question doesn't say on its own whose dove this is.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The Minty joke doesn't click. Minty's trait is carrying messages and checking on everyone, which isn't the core action here (women seeing someone and praising her). "I already know how this goes" leaves the baker asking "huh?" It also hints that the women react well, which helps rule out the wrong answers on the next card.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The card asks whether the queens and concubines are jealous, with False as the right answer. That treats a feeling the text never states (they aren't jealous) as fact. The text says only that they sing her praises (6:9). That detail is never told or asked anywhere, so the baker can leave Prep without it.

rule.text: Feelings: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: The verse 6:9 detail that the queens and concubines sing her praises is never told on a story card or tested directly. The baker can leave Prep missing it.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The setup compares the moment to the first night Papa Dorin saw the sky over his bakery. That points straight at the answer to card 8 ("Lights in the sky") and rules out "Gold in a fire" and "Gems in a crown."

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: "The question pictures her shining like what?" uses "The question" and "her" to point back to card 7, which is no longer on screen. The question should say which question is meant ("Who is this who shines...") and who it's about.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "The speaker knew exactly where that desire was leading" uses "that desire" and "The speaker" to point back to card 12. The question doesn't say on its own which desire it means (the speaker's visit to the walnut grove, and then ending up among the royal chariots).

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The English text of the Song never names its speakers. Stop 1 card 1 says plainly "Now he's the one talking" for 6:4-9. Stop 2 cards 7 and 10 say the text doesn't say who is speaking. papa-dorin.md#facts-and-scripture says to name who is speaking before quoting an "I." The "leave open what the text leaves open" rule only lists who is spoken to, why, and how two things connect. It doesn't cover the speaker.
findings.question: In the Song of Solomon, can Papa Dorin name speakers as he or she (the beloved or the darling) when the identity is only implied, or must he leave every speaker open? And when an "I" speaker can't be identified, as in 6:11-12, what should he say in place of naming them?
